questions.prompt: What is the top-level element of every JMeter test?
questions.explanation: Everything sits under the Test Plan. Thread Groups are children of it, samplers live in Thread Groups, and listeners are reporting elements.

questions.prompt: Which element actually sends a request to the system under test?
options: A sampler, such as HTTP Request
questions.explanation: Samplers generate requests and sample results. Listeners display results, config elements provide settings, and timers add delays.

questions.prompt: A listener only collects results from the samplers in its scope.
questions.explanation: Listeners follow the scoping rules: a listener under a Thread Group sees that group's samples; one at Test Plan level sees all.

questions.prompt: A sampler has a Response Assertion and a JSON Extractor as children. In which order do they run after the sample?
options: JSON Extractor (post-processor) first, then the Response Assertion
Response Assertion first, then the JSON Extractor
The order depends on which was added last
questions.explanation: Post-processors run before assertions in JMeter's execution order (config, pre-processors, timers, sampler, post-processors, assertions, listeners). That lets an assertion check a variable an extractor just set.

questions.prompt: A Thread Group has 10 threads, loop count 5 and three samplers. Each request takes about 200 ms and there are no timers. Roughly how many samples does the test produce?
questions.explanation: Each of the 10 threads runs the three samplers 5 times: 10 x 5 x 3 = 150. Response time affects duration, not the sample count.

questions.prompt: Which belong to the 'Pre-Processor' or 'Post-Processor' families? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Extractors are post-processors and User Parameters is a pre-processor. Constant Timer is a timer, its own family that runs before the sampler.

questions.prompt: Every request in this plan waits about 3 seconds even though only one 1-second Constant Timer is under the 'Search' sampler. Why?
questions.code:
Test Plan
  Thread Group
    Constant Timer (2000 ms)
    HTTP Request: Home
    HTTP Request: Search
      Constant Timer (1000 ms)
    HTTP Request: Product
options: The Thread Group-level timer applies to all three samplers and Search also gets its own: every sampler waits at least 2 s, Search waits 3 s
Timers run after the sampler, so delays accumulate across the loop
A Constant Timer of 2000 ms means 2 seconds per thread, divided by three samplers
The Test Plan has 'Run Thread Groups consecutively' ticked
questions.explanation: Timers in scope of a sampler are all applied and their delays are summed before that sampler. The group-level 2 s timer affects every sampler; Search also gets its own 1 s. Timers run before samplers, not after.

questions.prompt: Your plan has a login sampler with an extractor that saves `token`, and an assertion under login checks `${token}` is not empty. The assertion always fails even though the extractor works in later requests. What is the most likely mistake?
options: The assertion is a Response Assertion testing the response body for the literal text instead of testing the variable (it should use 'JMeter Variable' as field to test or a JSR223/size check on the variable)
Variables cannot be read in the same sampler
Extractors only run in GUI mode
questions.explanation: Post-processors run before assertions, so the variable is set in time; the usual error is asserting the wrong field. A Response Assertion can target a JMeter Variable as the field to test. Extractors run in every mode.

coding.title: Sort elements into execution order
coding.prompt:
JMeter runs elements in scope of a sampler in this order of **types**:
`config`, `preprocessor`, `timer`, `sampler`, `postprocessor`, `assertion`, `listener`.

Write `execution_order(elements)` where `elements` is a list of `(name, type)` tuples. Return the **names** sorted into execution order. Elements of the same type keep their original relative order.

Example: `[('Assert 200','assertion'), ('Login','sampler'), ('Defaults','config')]` returns `['Defaults', 'Login', 'Assert 200']`.
coding.explanation: Python's `sorted` is stable, so ranking by the type's position keeps same-type elements in tree order, which is exactly how JMeter treats several pre-processors or assertions.
hints: Write the order list once and use its index as the sort key.
`sorted` is stable, so ties keep their original order.
`sorted(elements, key=lambda e: ORDER.index(e[1]))` then take the names.

coding.title: Predict the sample count
coding.prompt:
Write `expected_samples(thread_groups)`. Each thread group is a dict `{'threads': int, 'loops': int, 'samplers': int}`. A loop count of `-1` means 'infinite' and cannot be predicted: in that case return `None` for the whole plan. Otherwise return the total samples of all groups.

Example: `[{'threads': 10, 'loops': 5, 'samplers': 3}]` returns `150`.
coding.explanation: Each thread runs every sampler once per loop, so threads x loops x samplers per group. Infinite loops are bounded only by duration, so the count is not knowable in advance. Checking the sample count after a run is a quick sanity test of a plan.
hints: Loop over the groups and multiply the three numbers.
Return `None` as soon as you meet a loop count of -1.
Sum the products of the finite groups.
